metadata.title: JZ Mock E · Paper 1
metadata.description: Worked steps, progressive hints and reviewed follow-up questions.

matches.rationale: Both require a parameterised quadratic to be strictly positive for every real input, using upward opening and a negative discriminant. The candidate has fixed leading coefficient, whereas the mock additionally checks a degree-zero leading parameter and excludes its linear case.

Both convert a global quadratic condition into a strict bound on its attained vertex height and then solve for the parameter. The candidate fixes downward opening and bounds a maximum; the mock bounds an upward minimum after checking the leading coefficient.

Both calculate a trapezium estimate and an exact geometric integral, then compare their difference. The candidate uses fixed semicircle ordinates and an underestimate; the mock uses a moving V-corner and solves a prescribed overestimate for the parameter.

Both calculate equally spaced boundary ordinates and apply endpoint/interior trapezium weights. The candidate additionally combines logarithms; it practises the numerical-estimate component, while the mock must also calculate true triangular area and solve an error equation.

Both eliminate the line variable to obtain a quadratic intersection equation and solve its parameter-discriminant restriction. The candidate allows touching and asks for a real parameter range; the mock requires two distinct circle intersections and counts integer parameters strictly inside the range.

Both replace a modulus by the correct formula on sign intervals before evaluating and combining the integral pieces. The candidate has one modulus and a possibly negative outside factor; the mock nests two moduli and uses nonnegative triangular pieces.

Both use modulus sign pieces and symmetry to calculate a finite geometric area, retaining the correct sign relative to the axis. The candidate has quadratic pieces and unknown axis crossings; the mock has nested linear modulus pieces with additional corners.

Both independently solve product-sign restrictions and intersect their intervals. The candidate uses polynomial factors; the mock additionally has denominator exclusions and mixed strict/non-strict endpoints before measuring the overlap.

Both solve two sign restrictions separately and take their intersection. The candidate then encodes that overlap as one quadratic inequality; the mock instead handles rational poles and measures the overlap length.

Both rewrite a rational power, differentiate at a contact point and build a line from a gradient and that point. The candidate requires a normal and intercept distance; the mock requires axis interchange before differentiation and reflecting the tangent equation back.

Both sum an infinite series by exposing repeating power-of-two structure and using a convergent geometric tail. The candidate groups repeated binary blocks (and its solution checks by scaled-copy subtraction); the mock must subtract scaled weighted terms to create the GP before applying its sum formula.

Both split a modulus-driven equation into quadratic cases and count only roots lying in their own branch, with boundary duplicates handled explicitly. The candidate branches by the input sign and classifies all possible counts; the mock first derives an area formula according to the moving corner and counts roots for its fixed condition.

Both justify triangle similarity, identify corresponding sides and use their common scale to recover an unknown length. The candidate uses parallel trapezium bases and diagonal parts; the mock uses repeated right-triangle altitudes and additionally sums their geometric progression.

Both recover a GP ratio from stated relations, check its magnitude is below one and calculate a sum to infinity. The candidate determines a surd ratio from term positions; the mock obtains its ratio from triangle similarity, so that geometric step is additional.

Both turn a signed-area condition with a variable endpoint into a polynomial parameter equation, evaluate it and reject roots incompatible with the original interval geometry. The candidate’s endpoint is a parabola root and its integral must vanish; the mock has a modulus corner and a nonzero target, so separate endpoint regions and duplicate roots matter.

Both eliminate simultaneous sine/cosine values, select their common quadrant and scale the whole angular period back to the original input before summing valid angles. The candidate gives a fixed angular interval; the mock instead uses an AP sum to determine the least endpoint. Distinct angle scales and constants require new calculations.

Both translate linked logarithmic/exponential identities to a common algebraic relation and use index/logarithm laws to recover a reciprocal expression. The candidate has variable bases and a power-of-power substitution; the mock has three fixed bases and combines reciprocals of the exponents with one common logarithm.

Both use an area condition to constrain side lengths and subtract two geometry equations sharing a height or known squared terms. The candidate compares two SSA triangles and recovers an angle; the mock concerns one AP-sided triangle with a fixed altitude and recovers its smallest side. The common-height elimination is the shared operation, not similarity.

Both treat a named quantity as a quadratic parameter, check the leading-coefficient domain and simplify a discriminant condition. The candidate isolates a repeated-root exception among supplied nonzero parameters; the mock derives the output range, includes repeated roots at its extrema and separately handles a zero output.

Both translate real quadratic roots into a discriminant inequality and preserve all parameter branches. The candidate seeks two distinct roots and plots a two-parameter region; the mock seeks at least one input for an output parameter, checks its zero-degree case and uses the resulting interval endpoints as extrema.

Both order the zeros of a trigonometric product, multiply factor signs interval by interval and respect boundary strictness. The candidate has two cosine factors and a strict negative set; the mock has a shifted/scaled cosine, sine and tangent, including a pole and a shared zero before measuring length.

Both find the zeros of a shifted sine factor and another trigonometric factor, build a product sign chart and keep valid zero endpoints. The mock adds a phase-scaled cosine and a tangent pole, so it is not the same two-factor equation or interval set.

Both find phase-sensitive trigonometric boundaries, combine factor signs and total the accepted interval lengths. The candidate asks for a fraction of the full interval using two factors; the mock has three factors, a domain pole and an isolated double zero, and asks the absolute length.

Both substitute two polynomial roots and eliminate terms between the resulting equations to recover a coefficient expression. The candidate provides both factor roots and solves a linear coefficient system; the mock must additionally derive and exhaust an integer product condition to discover its roots.

Both identify two graphs obtained by interchanging input and output and relate their enclosed geometric areas on a correctly restricted domain. The candidate can integrate its rational-power upper-minus-lower gap explicitly; the mock instead uses a given integral, the complementary endpoint rectangle and an additional horizontal reflection. This practises inverse-region geometry, not an unavailable logarithmic antiderivative.
